new_statements.quote: Stress is not distinctive in Yawuru, at least in the sense that no pairs of words are distinguished on the basis of different stress positions with otherwise identical sequences of segmental phonemes. Stress in Yawuru, however, is not completely predictable, either. [...] In the majority of words, primary stress (indicated by the acute accent mark) is assigned to the first syllable, regardless of the number of syllables or moras that make up the word. [p. 96] || There seem to be three principal regional dialects of the Yawuru language: 1) Jukun (or Northern), spoken by Minyjirr, Jukun and Walman groups; 2) Julbayi (or Southern Coastal) ...; 3) Marangan (or Eastern Inland) [p. 5]
new_statements.citation: Hosokawa, Komei. 1991. The Yawuru language of West Kimberley: a meaning-based description. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. (Yawuru grammar; Jukun treated as its Northern dialect.)
new_statements.locator: p. 96 (§3.7.1 Stress, §3.7.1.1 Primary stress; p. 128); fn. 130 p. 97; dialect statement p. 5 (§1.1.3.2, p. 37)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (556-pp. image scan, PDF page = printed page + 32) via the held scanned pin the page scan= printed p. 96). The passage is there verbatim under '3.7 Suprasegmental aspects / 3.7.1 Stress': "Stress is not distinctive in Yawuru, at least in the sense that no pairs of words are distinguished on the basis of different stress positions with otherwise identical sequences of segmental phonemes. Stress in Yawuru, however, is not completely predictable, either." and under '3.7.1.1 Primary stress': "In the majority of words, primary stress (indicated by the acute accent mark) is assigned to the first syllable, regardless of the number of syllables or moras that…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word in the great majority of words (1704 of 1730 nominals, over 98%, fn. 130 p. 97); stress is not contrastive but not fully predictable (onomatopoeia, interjections and some verb roots deviate). This is stated for Yawuru as a whole, whose data are chiefly from the Julbayi dialect; Jukun is classed as the Northern dialect and no Jukun-specific stress data are given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §3.7.1.2 (p. 98): 'Words with more than three syllables usually bear a secondary (or weaker) stress in addition to the primary stress'; mora-counting (sonorant moras): primary on the 1st mora, secondary on the 3rd mora if vocalic, otherwise on the 4th-mora vowel unless word-final; reduplicated words (§3.7.1.4, p. 102) put secondary stress on the first vowel of the repeated half.
new_statements.exceptions: c. 2% of nominals; onomatopoeic items, interjections and verb roots (fn. 130, p. 97). Stress 'not completely predictable'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms from a dictionary count of Yawuru nominals. Hosokawa says dialect differences 'chiefly consist in lexical forms' with a few phonological traits (Jukun drops final vowels, pp. 6-7); nothing on stress varying by dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Yawuru (Glottolog yawu1244), not Jukun as such. Hosokawa 1991: 5 classifies Jukun (Northern dialect: Minyjirr, Jukun, Walman groups) as one of three Yawuru dialects, while Glottolog, McGregor 1988 and Bates/Nekes & Worms treat Jukun/Dyugun (dyug1238) as a separate language. Hosokawa's stress data come chiefly from the Julbayi (Southern Coastal) dialect; he gives no Jukun-specific stress data, only lexical and final-vowel-dropping differences. No grammar, sketch or phonology of Jukun itself exists (McGregor 1988: 71 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None'; Stokes & McGregor 2003: 32).
